extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, and researchers interested in the 2020 Tokyo Olympics and its controversies
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style compilation of concerns, controversies, and standards/issues that arose around organising and running the 2020 Tokyo Summer Olympics (held in 2021). Covers health, environmental, legal, political, labour and organisational matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host legal obligation under guarantee G5.2
rubrics_metrics.description: Under guarantee G5.2 of the Contractual Framework for Hosting Olympic and Paralympic Games, the host country has the legal obligation to take all necessary measures to ensure that their Olympic-related activities should comply with any international agreements with regard to safety and health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a binding contractual/legal expectation on host governments to ensure safety and health compliance for Olympic activities; used to evaluate whether host actions met international safety/health obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: IOC anti-doping testing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The IOC regulations required extensive testing in the months prior to the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that the COVID-19 pandemic seriously affected doping tests (blood/urine) in advance of the games, and that reduced national testing capacity raised concerns about meeting IOC testing expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: FINA acceptable open-water temperature range
rubrics_metrics.description: FINA official competition water temperature acceptable range: 16–31 °C (61–88 °F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a technical safety standard for open-water events; the Odaiba venue water temperatures (~29–30 °C) were reported to be barely inside the acceptable range, prompting athlete and coach concerns and calls for venue relocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radiation safety level promise (0.23 μSv/hour)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Japanese government promised radiation levels below 0.23 μSv per hour for areas such as where the torch relay would begin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page records measured hotspots exceeding promised levels and criticises monitoring methodology (measuring only gamma, strategically placed posts, cleaned areas). Greenpeace and citizen maps provided alternative measurements—context for evaluating compliance with promised radiation thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: IOC guidelines prohibiting political gestures by athletes
rubrics_metrics.description: The IOC published three pages of guidelines prohibiting athletes from using political gestures, such as kneeling, hand gestures, and disrespect during medal ceremonies; athletes were allowed to express political views on traditional and social media, and in interviews outside the Olympic Village.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit behavioural rule for competitors; the article cites pushback and debate over political neutrality and the IOC's enforcement approach (case-by-case handling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sporting-body ban on Rising Sun Flag (example: FIFA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some sports bodies (e.g., FIFA) ban the Rising Sun Flag; sports organisers have policies restricting symbols deemed offensive or political.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes calls from South Korea and others to ban the flag at Olympic venues and cites existing bans by other organisations; contrasts such bans with the IOC's position (handled case-by-case).

rubrics_metrics.name: IOC case-by-case policy on political symbols/flags
rubrics_metrics.description: The IOC indicated that 'sports stadiums should be free of any political demonstration' and that concerns would be considered on a case-by-case basis rather than imposing blanket bans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the IOC's enforcement posture regarding politically sensitive symbols (e.g., Rising Sun Flag) and how that differs from uniform bans by other organisations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emblem selection procedural rules and IP vetting
rubrics_metrics.description: An Emblems Selection Committee organised an open call for design proposals open to Japanese residents over the age of 18; designs underwent intellectual property examinations before final approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recounts that initial emblem designs faced plagiarism allegations despite TOCOG saying the emblem passed IP examinations, leading to withdrawal and a public contest—illustrating procedural and IP-examination expectations for official insignia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition/remediation requirement for asbestos in venues
rubrics_metrics.description: Asbestos, a known health hazard and prohibited building material in many countries (including Japan), was found at the Tokyo Tatsumi International Swimming Center; organisers promised 'emergency countermeasures' after media coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presents a construction and public-health standard: materials prohibited by safety regulations must be removed or appropriately remediated; the page records initial government decisions and later promises to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worker-rights / overtime limits and safe working conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspectors found illegal overwork in almost 40 companies at construction sites, including workers with overtime >80 hours per month and cases exceeding 150 hours; patterns of 'dangerous overwork' were reported (e.g., up to 28 consecutive days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate compliance with labour law and occupational-safety standards; the BWI report and inspector findings are cited as evidence of systemic breaches and mistreatment of (including migrant) workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustainable procurement and food/wood standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics argued Tokyo failed to uphold procurement/ sustainability standards (examples cited: battery-cage-free eggs, gestation-crate-free pork, ecolabels in seafood and fresh produce) and that timber procurement from rainforests did not meet sustainability/rights criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are environmental and ethical procurement standards used to assess 'eco-friendly' claims; the article documents activist petitions, allegations of illegal logging, and criticisms of 'greenwashing'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-corruption / transparency expectations in bidding and sponsorship contracting
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectations that bid processes and sponsorship contracting be transparent and free from bribery; the article documents allegations of payments, missing accounting documents, arrests/indictments for bribery and bid-rigging, and Fair Trade Commission complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a governance/ethical standard for host bid and contracting practices—violations triggered investigations, resignations, arrests and later organisational consequences (e.g., Sapporo withdrawal from 2030 bid consideration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual property / originality expectations for designs and stadium plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations of plagiarism arose over the original Olympic emblem and later over elements of stadium design; organisers claimed IP examinations occurred, while critics and designers accused copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion relates to originality and respect for third-party IP in official designs; the article uses the emblem and stadium disputes to illustrate IP vetting limits and reputational risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat-safety scheduling and venue relocation to protect athletes
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of extreme summer heat, the IOC announced plans to move the Olympic marathon and race walking to Sapporo to avoid heat; other proposals included moving start times earlier (e.g., 5:00 a.m.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a safety-driven operational criterion: scheduling and venue choices should minimize heat exposure risks (hyperthermia) for athletes, staff and spectators. The page documents debates and local resistance around such changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water-quality standard (safe microbiological levels) for open-water venues
rubrics_metrics.description: High levels of faecally-derived coliform and E. coli bacteria were reported in the Odaiba Marine Park, prompting cancellation of test events and athlete complaints about odor and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though specific microbial threshold values are not quoted in the article, the incident is used to illustrate the expectation that open-water venues meet accepted water-quality/sanitation standards for athlete safety, and that failure may require venue changes or event cancellation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy vs. public-health transparency in reporting COVID-19 cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tokyo organising committee was criticised for not disclosing the nationality or gender of infected athletes for privacy reasons, while disclosing the number of athletes infected and the date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This represents a policy trade-off standard between individual privacy protections and public-health transparency during the pandemic; the article documents debate and athlete complaints about quarantine conditions.
